result:
In the beginning, there was a pause— a hush between inhalation and exhalation— where the mind hovered like a dragonfly above black water, seeing its own shimmering reflection distort and reform. I step into that pause now, summoning whatever words drift toward me from the swirling wind-tunnel of memory, dream, and half-captured possibility.  

Sometimes the first fragment I catch is not a word at all, but a scent— petrichor rising from cracked sidewalks after July rain. I remember being ten, barefoot, convinced that storms were conversations between clouds, loud arguments followed by tears of apology.  

Years later, in a city that never gives in to stillness, I pause beneath glass towers when thunderheads gather, letting the low sky inform me that disputes among giants are ongoing.  

A friend once said cities are organisms: their arteries flicker neon, their bones are steel, their voices echo through subway tunnels. If that is true, then nights are when the organism dreams, and midnight pedestrian murmurs are merely neurons firing.  

Tonight, I walk alone, hearing that collective brain sparking around me. A taxi horn becomes a synaptic snap; laughter spilling from a dim bar is dopamine in liquid form. I feel simultaneously contained by, and dissolved within, the breathing topology.  

Then the memory of another place rises— a coastline where gulls nested among rusted pilings. The air tasted of salt and woodsmoke, and conversations traveled differently, rounded by fog. I lived there one winter, convinced that if I listened long enough the sea would reveal an instruction manual for being alive.  

It never did, not in sentences, yet in the cadence of waves folding into themselves I sensed a recurring thesis: everything returns. Foam retreats but collects again; driftwood departs yet reappears, carved by distance into smoother syllables.  

I left that coast with pockets full of round stones, each one a small punctuation mark, comma or period, to be inserted later into paragraphs not yet imagined.  

Here, in the restless interior of a continent, those stones rest on my windowsill. Sunlight strikes them every morning, unlocking trapped glints of mica. Some mornings the reflection lands on the opposite wall like a slow telegraph, saying nothing explicit but reminding me that messages do not always require grammar.  

People complain that the world is overloaded with messages, yet often we starve for meaning. Between the two conditions lies a gulf where interpretation becomes art. Painters use color to question light; musicians bend time into loops; writers chase phantoms of sense across paper, hoping the shapes they corral will behave long enough for someone else to recognize their own pulse inside.  

Recognition is another storm. It crashes unexpectedly, eroding the dunes we arrange around the private sacred parts of ourselves. Sometimes I worry that too much understanding will strip away useful mysteries, leaving only fluorescent certainty, humming like an office light at midnight.  

On those nights I retreat to fiction. In invented cities, invented children chase invented dogs beneath invented moons, and I feel safer knowing none of it must endure the audit of fact-checkers. Paradoxically, within that latitude of untruths, I stumble over genuine feelings, the way someone walking backstage might discover the real theater only begins where the scenery ends.  

Years ago a teacher told me that literature is a kind of map, but he forgot to mention maps are never the territory. The thin blue line suggesting a river will not drench your boots; the dotted contour of a mountain has no altitude. And yet we treasure charts because our brains crave orientation.  

I carry several such maps in my head— favorite passages from Calvino, Le Guin, Bachmann, each line a coordinate pair I consult when lost. They do not resemble the streets I walk, yet by triangulating between them I reorient to myself, which is sometimes the harder destination.  

What, after all, is a self? A pronoun wearing accumulated anecdotes; a house whose rooms are furnished by other people’s sentences. I move through that house dusting off phrases, refolding memories, discarding obsolete metaphors like cracked teacups. Sometimes visitors come unannounced. A childhood friend appears in a doorway, asking if I still believe that clouds talk. I answer that I never stopped listening, but I grew polite enough not to interrupt them.  

Politeness, I suspect, is a negotiation between urge and silence. The city is rarely polite; it broadcasts its agenda in sirens and LED signage. Yet there are pockets where hush prevails: a library’s third floor at closing, or the interior of an all-night laundromat at four a.m., when dryers spin like warm planets, and everyone present pretends we are alone.  

In such refuges I often open a notebook and let sentences pour the way water finds lowest ground. The first lines are usually clumsy, like newborn foals, their knees shaking under untested weight. If I keep writing, muscle arrives; the passage stands. Later, revision will come as rain, erasing footprints, smoothing ruts, until only the essential rises to the surface.  

Essential. The word feels fragile, given how partial our perceptions remain. What seems crucial tonight may prove trivial next season. Still we chase essences because we hunger for anchors in a spinning solar storm.  

Speaking of storms, the thunder outside my window has begun. Streetlights blink, adjusting to sudden wind. Somewhere a dog announces its opinion. I pause mid-sentence, remembering the agreement between clouds I theorized as a child. Maybe they really are debating the architecture of tomorrow’s dawn. Maybe every argument in the sky resolves as sunrise.  

By the time these words find you, the storm will have drifted east, gifting another county its drama and scenting wheat fields with ozone. The stones on my windowsill will cool; their mica will wait for morning. I will sleep, perhaps dreaming of coastlines I have not yet visited, where someone very like you gathers round punctuation for narratives still unborn. And when I wake, I will open the window, invite the lightning-tinted air inside, and begin again. With gratitude for the rain.
